You pass with the chain in the right order, the right publisher for each arrow, and the one-parent rule. The right chain with one publisher wrong is a partial pass.

tf2 is the library that keeps a robot's frames as a tree: every named frame has at most one parent, and each edge between a parent and its child is a history of stamped transforms rather than one fixed number, published on
for anything that never does. A listener subscribes to both topics and keeps its own buffered history, so any node can ask the tree a question without owning any part of it.

The problem is that a robot's own position estimate has two different jobs that pull against each other: a controller needs a frame that never jumps so it can steer smoothly, and a planner needs one that never drifts so a saved map stays correct. One frame cannot be both, and a tree with a single parent per frame cannot let two different sources both claim to place the robot at once.
The tree resolves this by splitting the robot's world position into two edges. Odometry publishes
, drifting smoothly as small errors add up. Localisation publishes
, the correction that makes the chain agree with the map, free to jump whenever a new estimate arrives, because
as its one parent and cannot take

as a second. A lookup asks for one frame's pose in another by walking the tree to their common ancestor and composing the edges along the way, interpolating between stored times for anything in motion, and refusing outright to guess beyond the oldest or newest time it has stored.

What goes wrong under pressure rarely looks like an error naming the real cause. A lookup for the current time can fail complaining about extrapolating into the future when a transform has not arrived yet, or into the past once one side's clock and the other's have drifted decades apart. And the quietest failure throws nothing at all: asking for the newest transform available returns one however old it is, so a broadcaster that has died still answers every query with its last known pose, and only comparing that transform's own timestamp against the current time catches it.
